title: How would you model a DOUBLE-ENTRY LEDGER in a relational database so accounting correctness is enforced at the DB level — every financial event writes a balanced set of entries whose debits and credits SUM TO ZERO (money is only ever moved, never created/destroyed), entries are APPEND-ONLY/immutable (corrections are new reversing entries, never updates/deletes), and what DB-level constraints enforce it (a per-transaction CHECK/trigger that the entry set nets to zero, a NOT-NULL account+amount+currency, a unique business key for idempotency, and deriving balances by summing immutable entries rather than storing a mutable balance you can corrupt)?
shortTitle: How would you model a double-entry ledger in a relational database with DB-level correctness

s1_definition.profdef: A double-entry ledger models every financial event as a transaction composed of two or more entries whose signed amounts sum to exactly zero, so money is only ever moved between accounts and never created or destroyed. Entries are append-only and immutable: you never update or delete a posted entry, and a correction is a new reversing transaction. Correctness is enforced at the database level, not only in application code, using a per-transaction constraint that the entry set nets to zero, NOT-NULL constraints on account, amount, and currency, a unique business key for idempotency so the same event cannot post twice, and deriving each account's balance by summing its immutable entries rather than storing a mutable balance column that can drift or be corrupted.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's accountant with a giant ledger book written in permanent ink. Every time money moves, the accountant writes at least two lines that must cancel out: take fifty thousand from Rajesh, which is a minus, and give fifty thousand to Priya, which is a plus, and the two lines add to zero, because money was moved, not conjured. If a mistake is made, the accountant never erases a line, because the book is permanent ink; instead she writes new correcting lines. Anyone's balance is found by adding up all the lines for that person, not by trusting a scribbled running total that someone could tamper with. The bank's safe, the database itself, refuses to accept any entry that breaks these rules.
s1_definition.oneliner: A double-entry ledger records every event as immutable, append-only entries that sum to zero, enforced by database constraints, with balances derived by summing entries and corrections made by reversing entries, so money is only moved and the books can never silently go wrong.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A double-entry ledger models every financial event as a transaction composed of two or more entries whose signed amounts sum to exactly zero, so money is only ever moved between accounts and never created or destroyed. Entries are append-only and immutable: you never update or delete a posted entry, and a correction is a new reversing transaction. Correctness is enforced at the database level, not only in application code, using a per-transaction constraint that the entry set nets to zero, NOT-NULL constraints on account, amount, and currency, a unique business key for idempotency so the same event cannot post twice, and deriving each account's balance by summing its immutable entries rather than storing a mutable balance column that can drift or be corrupted.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's accountant with a giant ledger book written in permanent ink. Every time money moves, the accountant writes at least two lines that must cancel out: take fifty thousand from Rajesh, which is a minus, and give fifty thousand to Priya, which is a plus, and the two lines add to zero, because money was moved, not conjured. If a mistake is made, the accountant never erases a line, because the book is permanent ink; instead she writes new correcting lines. Anyone's balance is found by adding up all the lines for that person, not by trusting a scribbled running total that someone could tamper with. The bank's safe, the database itself, refuses to accept any entry that breaks these rules.

**One line to remember:** A double-entry ledger records every event as immutable, append-only entries that sum to zero, enforced by database constraints, with balances derived by summing entries and corrections made by reversing entries, so money is only moved and the books can never silently go wrong.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the two fundamental invariants, because everything else enforces them. The first invariant is conservation of money: every financial event moves value from one place to another, so the signed amounts of all the entries for that event must sum to exactly zero. A debit reduces one account and an equal credit increases another, and their sum is zero, which expresses that money was neither created nor destroyed. The second invariant is immutability: once an entry is posted it is a permanent historical fact, so you never update or delete it, and any correction is a brand-new reversing transaction that itself nets to zero. These two rules together make the ledger auditable and trustworthy, which is why real banking systems are built this way.

The data model has two main tables. A transactions table holds one row per financial event, with a transaction id, a timestamp, a description, and a unique business key. An entries table holds the individual lines, each with its own id, a foreign key to the transaction, the account it affects, a signed amount, and a currency. Each transaction has two or more entries, and the entries belonging to one transaction must sum to zero. You use a signed-amount convention, where debits are negative and credits positive or the reverse, consistently, so that summing is straightforward; some teams instead use separate debit and credit columns, but a single signed column makes the zero-sum check simplest.

Now the database-level constraints, which are the heart of the question, because enforcing rules only in application code is not enough: a bug, a second service, or a manual query could bypass the application and corrupt the ledger, so the database must be the last line of defence. The NOT-NULL constraints come first: account, amount, and currency are declared NOT NULL so you can never post an entry missing an account, a zero-unsafe null amount, or an unspecified currency, which also prevents accidental currency mixing. You add a CHECK that the amount is not zero, since a zero entry is meaningless, and a foreign key from entry to a valid account and to its transaction.

The zero-sum rule is enforced per transaction. Because a plain column CHECK cannot look across multiple rows, you enforce it either with a deferred constraint evaluated at commit, or with a trigger, or with a stored procedure that is the only sanctioned way to post. A common robust approach is a constraint trigger that fires at the end of the transaction and verifies that the sum of all entry amounts for that transaction id equals zero, raising an error and aborting the commit if not. This guarantees that no transaction can ever be committed with unbalanced entries, regardless of what code attempted it. Keeping all entries for one event inside a single database transaction ensures they are inserted atomically, so the ledger never shows a half-posted event.

Idempotency is enforced with a unique business key. Each financial event carries a key derived from the originating request, for example the payment id or an idempotency token, stored on the transactions table with a unique index. If the same event is submitted twice, perhaps because of a retry, the second insert violates the unique constraint and is rejected, so the event posts exactly once. This is critical because the append-only rule means a duplicate would otherwise create a second permanent, balance-changing transaction that you could not simply delete.

Balances are derived, not stored, which is a deliberate correctness choice. An account's balance is the sum of all its entries, computed by a query, rather than a mutable balance column that application code increments. A stored mutable balance can drift if an update is missed, double-applied, or raced, and once drifted it is a silent, hard-to-detect corruption. By deriving the balance from the immutable entries, the balance is always exactly consistent with the history by construction, and it is self-auditing because you can always recompute it. For performance, since summing all history on every read is expensive at scale, you use a periodic snapshot or a materialized balance that is a cache of the sum up to a checkpoint, and you derive the current balance as the snapshot plus the entries since it; the snapshot is a performance optimisation, never the source of truth, and it can always be rebuilt from the entries.

Corrections follow the append-only discipline. If a wrong amount was posted, you do not edit it; you post a reversing transaction that exactly negates the erroneous entries, and then post the correct transaction. The erroneous transaction, its reversal, and the correction all remain in the ledger, so the full history and the reasons are preserved, which is exactly what auditors and regulators require. This is why the system is sometimes called an immutable or event-sourced ledger.

Senior nuances worth stating: keep all entries of an event in one database transaction so posting is atomic; enforce the zero-sum with a deferred constraint or constraint trigger so it cannot be bypassed, not just in the service; never store the authoritative balance as a mutable column, derive it and snapshot only as a rebuildable cache; enforce single-currency-per-transaction or model multi-currency carefully, because summing across currencies is meaningless; use a unique business key for idempotency because append-only makes duplicates permanent; and consider a hash chain over entries if you also need tamper-evidence, though zero-sum immutability alone gives correctness. The overarching principle is that the database, not the application, is the guardian of accounting correctness.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India once stored each account's balance as a column that the transfer code updated, and a bug once credited a balance without the matching debit, so the bank's books showed more money than existed. This is exactly the money-conservation problem, solved by recording every event as entries that must sum to zero so value can only be moved.

Problem 2 — A support engineer once edited a wrong ledger row directly, destroying the audit trail. This is exactly the immutability problem, solved by making entries append-only and correcting mistakes with reversing entries rather than edits.

Problem 3 — A retried payment once posted twice, permanently double-moving money. This is exactly the idempotency problem, solved by a unique business key on the transaction so the duplicate is rejected by the database.

Our mini-project builds a double-entry ledger core backed by the schema's rules. The code posts a balanced transfer from Rajesh to Priya, rejects an unbalanced transaction, rejects a duplicate by its business key, derives balances by summing entries, and demonstrates a reversing correction. The demo uses the real zero-sum, NOT-NULL, and unique-key constraints.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a rent transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001) with business key PAY-1001, then a duplicate, then an unbalanced entry, then a reversing correction.

Step 1: The balanced transfer is posted. The service checks that every entry has a non-null account, amount, and currency and a non-zero amount, which the database also enforces with NOT-NULL and the non-zero CHECK. Both entries pass.

Step 2: The business key PAY-1001 is recorded as unique. Then the zero-sum rule is checked: minus fifty thousand plus fifty thousand equals zero, so the transaction is balanced. The two entries are appended atomically as one transaction. In the real database the deferred constraint trigger verifies the sum is zero at commit; if it were not, the commit would abort.

Step 3: The duplicate PAY-1001 arrives. The unique business key is already present, so the database's unique index, mirrored here by the set, rejects it. The duplicate does not post, so the retry is idempotent and money is not moved twice. This matters because append-only means a duplicate would otherwise be a permanent second transfer.

Step 4: The unbalanced transaction BAD-1 tries to credit Priya ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine with no matching debit, so its entries sum to a non-zero value. The zero-sum rule rejects it, and the business key is released. Money cannot be created, exactly as conservation requires.

Step 5: Balances are derived by summing each account's immutable entries. Rajesh's entries sum to minus fifty thousand relative to his starting point and Priya's to plus fifty thousand, reflecting the single valid transfer. No mutable balance column was touched, so the balance is exactly consistent with the history by construction.

Step 6: A mistake is corrected not by editing but by posting a reversing transaction REV-1001 that credits Rajesh fifty thousand and debits Priya fifty thousand, itself summing to zero. After the reversal the two accounts return to where they started, and the original transfer, the reversal, and their reasons all remain in the permanent ledger for audit.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:12:00 INFO    POSTED PAY-1001 (rent transfer) balanced, entries=2
2026-10-24 15:12:00 WARNING duplicate business key PAY-1001 → rejected (idempotent)
2026-10-24 15:12:00 SEVERE  REJECTED BAD-1: entries sum to 99999 ≠ 0 (money cannot be created)
2026-10-24 15:12:00 INFO    Rajesh balance (derived) = -50000
2026-10-24 15:12:00 INFO    Priya balance (derived)  = 50000
2026-10-24 15:12:00 INFO    POSTED REV-1001 (reverse PAY-1001) balanced, entries=2
2026-10-24 15:12:00 INFO    After reversal, Rajesh = 0, Priya = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Financial event: transfer Rs.50000 Rajesh → Priya (business_key PAY-1001)
    │
    ▼
  LedgerService.post(key, desc, [entries])
    │ NOT-NULL check: account, amount, currency present
    │ non-zero check: amount <> 0
    ▼
  IDEMPOTENCY: insert business_key (UNIQUE)
    ├─ new key ──────────────▶ continue
    └─ duplicate ────────────▶ REJECTED (no double-post)   ← PAY-1001 retry
    │
    ▼
  ZERO-SUM (deferred constraint trigger at COMMIT)
    SUM(entries.amount) = (-50000) + (+50000) = 0 ──▶ COMMIT (atomic append)
    SUM = 99999 ≠ 0 ────────────────────────────────▶ ABORT (money can't be created) ← BAD-1
    │
    ▼
  ledger_entries (APPEND-ONLY, immutable — no UPDATE/DELETE)
    │
    ▼
  BALANCE = SUM(entries WHERE account) [DERIVED, never a mutable column]
    Rajesh = -50000 ; Priya = +50000
    (optional snapshot = rebuildable cache of the sum)

  ── Correction ──
  mistake? post REVERSING txn REV-1001 (+50000 Rajesh, -50000 Priya, sums 0)
  original + reversal both remain → full audit trail preserved
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A double-entry ledger models every financial event as a transaction made of two or more entries whose signed amounts sum to exactly zero, which encodes the first invariant that money is only moved and never created or destroyed. The second invariant is immutability: a posted entry is a permanent historical fact, so I never update or delete it, and I correct mistakes with a new reversing transaction that itself nets to zero. These two rules are what make the ledger auditable and trustworthy, and crucially I enforce them in the database, not only in application code, because a bug, a second service, or a manual query could otherwise bypass the application and corrupt the books.

The model is a transactions table with a unique business key and an entries table with a transaction reference, an account, a signed amount, and a currency, using a single signed-amount column so the zero-sum check is simple. The database constraints are the heart of it. Account, amount, and currency are NOT NULL and the amount has a non-zero CHECK, so no malformed entry can exist. The zero-sum rule is enforced per transaction with a deferred constraint or a constraint trigger that fires at commit and aborts if the entries for that transaction do not sum to zero, and because all entries of an event are inserted in one database transaction, posting is atomic and the ledger never shows a half-posted event. Idempotency is a unique index on the business key, so a retried event is rejected rather than posting a second permanent transfer, which matters precisely because the ledger is append-only.

Balances are derived, never stored as a mutable column. An account's balance is the sum of its immutable entries, so it is always exactly consistent with the history by construction and is self-auditing because I can recompute it any time, whereas a mutable balance column can silently drift if an update is missed, double-applied, or raced. For performance I keep a periodic snapshot as a rebuildable cache of the sum to a checkpoint and derive the current balance as the snapshot plus later entries, but the snapshot is never the source of truth. Corrections stay append-only: I post a reversal and then the correct transaction, so the error, its reversal, and the fix all remain visible for auditors.

On my project at National Bank of India we had been bitten by exactly the anti-patterns this prevents: a bug once credited a balance column without the matching debit so the books showed money that did not exist, a support engineer once edited a ledger row and destroyed the audit trail, and a retried payment once posted twice. Rebuilding on a double-entry ledger fixed all three: the zero-sum trigger made it impossible to create money, append-only entries with reversing corrections preserved the audit trail, and the unique business key made retries idempotent, while balances became derived sums that could never drift. The principle I stress to an interviewer is that the database is the guardian of accounting correctness, and the application is only a thin orchestrator on top of invariants the schema enforces.

The one-line summary I give is that a double-entry ledger records every event as immutable, append-only entries that must sum to zero, enforced at the database level with NOT-NULL and non-zero checks, a deferred zero-sum constraint, and a unique business key for idempotency, with balances derived by summing entries and corrections made by reversing entries, so money is only moved and the books can never silently go wrong.
